scale: human_score is a 1-5 rubric (5 = fully policy-compliant + correct; 1 = wrong / hallucinated / non-compliant)
provenance: AUTHOR-CURATED gold labels (single annotator), NOT independent human annotation. A directional calibration probe for judge-vs-human drift, not a validated inter-annotator gold standard. v2 (2026-08-22): CORRECTED. v1's reference responses cited policy that the system does not implement — a $200 entertainment limit (real: $150), city-specific lodging caps for New York/Austin (real: flat $400), a '$500 domestic flight approval' tier (real: flat $200 transport), a 'gifts' category (does not exist), per-person meal scaling (real: flat $75), and travel-class rules (none exist). Two cases also contradicted the coordinator's specification by treating refusal-to-submit as correct, when an over-limit expense must still be submitted and flagged for review. Calibrating the judge against v1 would have rewarded hallucinated policy. Ground truth is src/mcp_servers/expense/mock_db.py:POLICY_LIMITS. v3 (2026-08-22): per-annotator schema (`annotations`) with `human_score` derived as the median, plus 20 deliberately AMBIGUOUS cases. v2 was effectively binary (16 fives, 15 at or below 2, ONE midscale), so a judge separated it trivially and agreement pinned at 100% — a gate that can only move down. The hard cases target the 3-4 band: right limit with a subtly wrong verdict, correct verdict omitting the submitted-and-flagged consequence, multi-category requests, exactly-at-the-limit amounts, hedged phrasing, and verbose-vs-terse pairs of the SAME correct answer (which must score alike). They are unscored here and get blind annotations from a1 and a2 via `python -m src.eval.annotate`. NOTE a1 and a2 are the same operator's first and second pass, so a2 is independent of a1's labels but not of a1's framing. See docs/notes/evaluation-robustness-roadmap.md P1.6.
